analysis.one_liner: Wipes out EPA limits on carbon pollution from power plants and blocks similar rules for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 81 cosponsors, it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have erased three EPA proposals limiting greenhouse gas emissions from power plants — the proposals that later became the Clean Power Plan — and barred the EPA from issuing any similar rule for five years unless Congress passed a law specifically allowing it. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies and coal-fired power plant operators, who would have avoided the emission limits and could keep burning coal without new federal restrictions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal companies and coal-fired power plants

how_it_helps.text: Nullifies three proposed EPA rules limiting greenhouse gas emissions from existing, new, and modified or reconstructed power plants, giving them no force or effect.
Bars the EPA for five years from issuing or implementing any rule substantially similar to the nullified rules unless a federal law specifically authorizes it.

analysis.who_pays: People living downwind of coal plants, who would face more of the pollution those rules were meant to cut, and the public bearing the costs of unchecked power-plant carbon emissions — from health effects to climate damage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Downwind communities and the general public

drawbacks.text: The EPA rules the bill targeted were designed to cut carbon emissions from power plants, the country's largest single source of greenhouse gases, so killing them removes a tool for limiting those emissions.
The bill would have overridden the EPA's proposed rules by statute before the agency's own rulemaking process — including public comment and finalization — could run its course.

The honest cost an opponent would acknowledge: coal-dependent regions of West Virginia and other states argued the rules threatened coal mining jobs and could raise electricity costs, which is why the bill drew broad Republican support and a Democratic cosponsor from a coal state.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's only real effect is removing pollution limits on power plants for at least five years. The benefits go to the coal and utility industries that would have borne compliance costs; the costs — more carbon emissions and the pollutants that come with burning coal — fall on the public. There is no offsetting consumer protection or rate relief in the bill text.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee on June 13, 2014, and died there with no hearing, markup, or vote when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. David McKinley introduced the bill on June 9, 2014, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On June 13, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power — the last action ever taken on it.
The bill attracted 81 cosponsors: 80 Republicans and 1 Democrat.
No further action was recorded before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public interest in limiting power-plant carbon pollution, since the EPA rules the bill targeted were never nullified by it. Coal operators hoping to avoid the emission limits did not get the relief they sought from this bill.

for.name: Rep. David McKinley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the EPA's proposed power-plant carbon rules.

for.name: 1 of 201 House Democrats
for.role: House Democratic cosponsor (Rep. Nick Rahall of West Virginia)

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Fred Upton (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Power Subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or floor vote; the bill died there.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Backed the EPA's power-plant carbon rules and opposed legislation to block them, threatening vetoes of similar measures.

sides.party_line_note: All but one of the 81 cosponsors were Republicans; the single Democrat, Nick Rahal of West Virginia, represented a coal-producing state. There was never a vote to measure the full chambers.

industries.note: Nullifying the EPA rules would keep coal-fired plants buying and burning coal without federal emission limits, protecting demand for coal. The cost lands on people breathing the resulting pollution.
Plant operators would avoid the compliance costs and planning the proposed rules required. Their savings come at the expense of emission reductions the rules were designed to deliver.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and natural gas producers
industries.note: Without carbon limits on power plants, the shift away from coal toward cleaner generation slows, reducing the market opportunity for lower-emitting electricity sources. Their interest in this fight runs with cleaner air.
